learner.prompt: Design note synchronization for an offline field-inspection app. Propose alternatives, defend one, and show how it behaves under failure.
learner.material: Fifty staff create or edit up to 10,000 text notes per device. Each note body is at most 2 KiB. Devices can be offline for 48 hours. Requests and responses can be lost, duplicated or reordered.
constraints: Persist a local save before displaying 'saved on this device'; target p95 completion within 100 ms under the stated local workload and measure that target.
Display 'synced' only after server durable acknowledgement.
A crash after a displayed durable save must not lose that saved note under the stated storage assumptions.
Retries must not create duplicate logical edits.
Concurrent edits from different devices must remain recoverable without silent overwrite.
State storage assumptions, unresolved tradeoffs, and a validation plan.

reviewer_only.attempt: I would send each edit immediately and retry with a new request ID if there is no response. The last arriving version wins.
reviewer_only.failed_hypothesis: No response proves the server did not save the edit.
reviewer_only.prediction_probe: Predict the outcome if the server commits an edit but its response is lost, and the client retries.
hint_ladder: Trace a save across local commit, server commit and acknowledgement.
A lost acknowledgement does not tell you whether the server committed; retry identity and version conflicts matter.
Commit the note plus an outbox item locally, reuse one operation ID on retries, and atomically deduplicate on the server.

worked_outcome.assumptions: Local and server storage honor committed durable transactions across process crashes; hardware destruction and storage corruption are outside this scenario.
worked_outcome.design: A local transaction saves the note, its base revision, and an outbox operation with a stable ID. Show local saved after commit. Retry that same operation until the server atomically records its ID and a durable version; return the original result for duplicate IDs. Reject inconsistent reuse of an ID. Show synced only after its durable acknowledgement, then transactionally mark the outbox item complete. A stale base revision stores a conflict branch linked to its parent; retain both versions and request an explicit merge rather than silently choosing a winner.
worked_outcome.alternative: A client may retain an unacknowledged conflict locally instead of server branch storage if it clearly reports that status, preserves both edits, and defines later resolution. Last-arrival overwrite violates the stated requirement.
failure_timelines: Crash before local commit: saved was not displayed; after commit: note and outbox recover together.
Server commit then lost response: retrying the stable ID returns the same committed result without another edit.
Out-of-order delivery: base revisions identify stale edits and retain a conflict instead of overwriting.
Crash after acknowledgement but before local outbox cleanup: replay is harmless through server deduplication.
worked_outcome.validation: Inject crashes at each transaction boundary; duplicate, drop and reorder traffic; edit the same note on two devices; assert recoverability, deduplication and correct UI statuses. Measure local-save p95 on representative devices with 10,000 notes before claiming the 100 ms target.
worked_outcome.capacity: 10,000 maximum-size note bodies occupy about 19.53 MiB before metadata, indexes, revisions and queued edits; measure additional growth and define retention explicitly.

checks: Trace the lost-response retry with one stable operation ID and atomic server deduplication.
Show local-save and server-sync as distinct states backed by commits.
Demonstrate both concurrent versions remain accessible.
Cover each failure timeline and provide a measurable latency validation plan.
Do not claim latency measurements or absolute hardware durability from the design alone.
reviewer_only.transfer_question: Can receiving an HTTP request alone justify displaying 'synced'?
reviewer_only.transfer_answer: No. The acknowledgement must mean the server committed durable data; receiving or queuing a request is insufficient.
